items.q: What is the core difference between compiling and interpreting?
options: Interpreted languages never produce any machine code at any point
A compiler translates the whole program to machine code ahead of time; an interpreter carries out the source as it runs
Compiled languages don't need a CPU
Compiling runs the program; interpreting only checks it for errors

explain.right: Compiling translates everything up front into a runnable file; interpreting translates and executes the source while running.
explain.wrong: Both ultimately result in machine code running on the CPU; interpreting isn't just error-checking, and all programs need a CPU.

items.q: Machine code is best described as:
options: Simple numeric instructions a specific CPU executes directly
Another word for the Python or JavaScript you type
A universal format every CPU runs identically

explain.right: Machine code is the low-level numeric instructions the CPU runs directly, and it's specific to a CPU architecture (x86 vs ARM differ).
explain.wrong: It isn't your high-level source or comments, and it isn't universal; different architectures have different machine codes.

items.q: At the lowest level, a CPU runs programs by repeatedly doing what?
options: Guessing the answer and checking later
Reading the whole program into one giant instruction and solving it
Asking the operating system to think for it
Fetch an instruction, decode it, execute it, then move to the next — over and over

explain.right: The CPU repeats the fetch-decode-execute cycle billions of times a second, advancing through instructions in memory.
explain.wrong: It doesn't solve a program in one step or outsource thinking; everything is tiny sequential instructions.

items.q: Someone says 'Python is interpreted, so no compiling ever happens.' What's the accurate correction?
options: CPython compiles your source to bytecode first, then runs that bytecode — translating happens, just as part of running
Python actually compiles to a standalone .exe every time

explain.right: CPython compiles source to bytecode (the __pycache__ .pyc files) and then executes it, so 'interpreted' means translating happens during running, not that none happens.
explain.wrong: It doesn't produce a standalone binary each run, and it still ultimately runs on the CPU; the blanket 'no compiling' claim is the misconception.

items.q: Explain, in a sentence or two, the path from the Python you write to something a CPU can actually run.
rubric: Mentions translation to a lower level (bytecode and/or machine code), compiled ahead of time or as it runs
Ends with the CPU executing machine instructions (fetch-decode-execute)

explain.right: Good answers trace source → translated to lower-level instructions → CPU executes machine code step by step.
explain.wrong: A weak answer says 'the computer just reads Python' without any translation step or the CPU running machine code.
